sum: Arista Networks heads into its third-quarter earnings release with a stronger revenue outlook but a higher bar for execution. In a report published Thursday, October 29, 24/7 Wall St. said investors will weigh AI networking demand, margins and supply conditions when the company reports on November 3.
Arista Networks stock traded at 157.82 euros on Lang & Schwarz at 10:39 CET on Friday, October 30, 2026; the real-time quote of Arista Networks stock is available here.

Arista generated 3.04 billion US dollars of revenue in the second quarter, an increase of 37.7 percent from a year earlier, according to the 24/7 Wall St. report. Non-GAAP earnings per share reached 1.02 US dollars, ahead of the 0.89 US dollar consensus cited in the article.

The result marked Arista's first quarterly revenue above 3 billion US dollars. Management raised its fiscal 2026 revenue guidance to 12.6 billion US dollars from 11.5 billion US dollars in May, implying 40 percent growth. Deferred revenue rose to 6.9 billion US dollars, while purchase commitments reached 9.7 billion US dollars.

For the third quarter, management guided to revenue of about 3.3 billion US dollars, gross margin of about 63 percent and non-GAAP earnings per share of 1.06 to 1.08 US dollars. The report said the margin picture will be closely watched after second-quarter gross margin fell to 63.4 percent from 65.6 percent a year earlier, partly reflecting customer mix and tariff refunds.

Chief Executive Jayshree Ullal said price increases would help only toward the end of 2026 or in 2027 as memory and silicon costs rise. Management also expects Microsoft and Meta Platforms to anchor one or two customers accounting for at least 10 percent of revenue and warned that industry component shortages could persist until 2028.

AI networking remains the central growth theme. Arista has more than 100 cumulative Etherlink customers and targets at least 3.5 billion US dollars of AI fabrics revenue in 2026. The company also expects 1.6-terabit switches to enter trials in the second half of 2026, with production scheduled for 2027.

sum: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com.

Arista Networks (ANET) turns more of its revenue into operating profit than any of the five networking and hardware companies in its peer group. Only Dell Technologies posted faster revenue growth. Over the past year, however, Arista shares have gained less than four of those five rivals, and its P/E sits in the middle of the group. So what do you get for Arista’s price that its rivals do not offer?

Compared with Ciena (CIEN), Arista offers the same growth and far more profit at a lower price for each dollar of earnings. Ciena, another communications equipment maker, grew revenue 32.6% over its latest four fiscal quarters. Arista posted that exact rate over its own four quarters. Arista turned 43.1% of its revenue into operating profit, against 14.1% for Ciena. Ciena’s P/E is still higher, at 78.4, compared with 57.4 for Arista.
The share prices tell a different story. Over the past year, Ciena stock rose 108.7%, while Arista stock climbed 25.8%.

Rivals that cost less than Arista either grew more slowly or retained far less of every sales dollar. Cisco Systems trades at 31.9 times earnings, but its revenue grew 11.8%. Hewlett Packard Enterprise also sits below Arista on both metrics. Dell Technologies is the one rival that grew faster, at 49.0%, and it trades at 27.5 times earnings. Dell, like Hewlett Packard Enterprise, is a technology hardware maker, a different kind of business, and it kept 9.6% of its revenue as operating profit.

sum: Arista published its batch of security advisories on September 9, turning an advance warning into an immediate customer maintenance task. The release includes critical vulnerabilities affecting EOS and VeloCloud. Cisco's September 4 security commentary describes the broader problem: vulnerability discovery is accelerating beyond customers' ability to remediate it.

For Cisco Systems, Inc. (NASDAQ:CSCO) and Arista Networks, Inc. (NYSE:ANET), that creates an investment question beyond port speeds. Can suppliers keep expanding AI networks without letting the cost and disruption of securing them erode customer confidence?

Cisco says it scanned 1.8 billion lines of code across 25 languages in eight weeks using frontier models. Its September 2 advisories already include critical issues involving IOS XR and Nexus 9000 switches using Silicon One. Customers have been directed to fixed software.

That is a potential advantage if earlier detection prevents expensive incidents. Cisco's breadth across networking, security and support could also help customers coordinate their response. Yet finding defects creates engineering and service obligations before it creates incremental revenue. Entitlement to free security upgrades makes it especially risky to treat every patch as a paid refresh.

Arista's updated summary lists critical EOS gNPSI and P4Runtime vulnerabilities with CVSS v3.1 scores of 10, alongside other findings. Customers must assess the conditions and remediation for their own environments. Severity scores alone do not establish exploitation or an earnings loss. Its May statement also says AI-assisted testing caught complex flaws before software release, evidence that better detection can prevent some customer exposure.

For Arista Networks, Inc. (NYSE:ANET), consolidating updates into maintenance windows could strengthen its appeal to customers running demanding networks. The bear case is that testing and deployment consume resources that customers otherwise devote to expansion. Cisco Systems, Inc. Management has already warned investors to anticipate “gross margin pressure” as it pays more to secure the parts it needs.

sum: The company’s incredible AI-driven growth is undeniable, but it rests on a surprisingly narrow foundation that every investor should understand.

Arista Networks (ANET) stock has been on a strong run, rewarding shareholders with a gain of 61% in the last 12 months and sitting near its high. The story is strong: the company is a key player in the AI infrastructure buildout, and management reports that demand is the strongest they have ever seen.

But beneath the surface of this success lies a single, concentrated risk. The concern stems from the source of the company’s revenue, rather than the total revenue or margins that everyone watches. For Arista, a large slice of the pie comes from just two customers.

In its most recent full year, Arista disclosed that its top 2 customers, identified by the CEO as long-term partners Microsoft and Meta, accounted for a significant portion of its business. Specifically, management stated that Customers A and B accounted for 16–20% of our overall business.

Think about that for a moment. That portion of Arista’s entire operation hinges on the spending decisions of 2 companies. While these are deep, multi-year partnerships, such customer concentration creates a structural vulnerability. A single decision made in one of their boardrooms—to pause a data center buildout, to shift capital priorities, or to develop an in-house alternative—could directly reduce a substantial portion of Arista’s revenue growth.

This concentration risk is particularly notable because of the high expectations baked into Arista’s stock price. The stock currently trades at a price-to-earnings multiple of 55.5, which is toward the top of its own 10-year range. Its price-to-sales ratio of 21.3 is similarly stretched, sitting just shy of its decade high of 21.7.

A valuation this high suggests the market is pricing in more than simple growth; it expects smooth, uninterrupted growth. It leaves very little room for error.
